ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached circuit diagram shows a single-transistor common-emitter amplifier. The input is coupled through capacitor C1 to the transistor base. R1 and R2 form the base bias network. R3 is connected from the collector to +Ucc. The output is taken from the collector through coupling capacitor C2. The emitter is connected to ground through resistor R4, and capacitor CE is drawn in parallel with R4 as an emitter bypass capacitor. Reasoning: Since CE is connected across the emitter resistor R4, when CE is present it bypasses R4 for AC signals, reducing emitter degeneration and giving a relatively high midband voltage gain magnitude. After disconnecting CE, R4 is no longer bypassed and remains in the AC emitter path. This adds emitter degeneration/negative feedback and increases the effective denominator in the common-emitter gain expression, so the amplifier voltage gain magnitude becomes smaller.

raw_record.question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, how will the voltage gain of the amplifier change after disconnecting the capacitor \(C_E\)?

method.method_draft: From the image, note that CE bypasses the emitter resistor R4 in a common-emitter stage. Treat C1 and C2 as coupling capacitors and compare midband small-signal gain. With CE connected, R4 is effectively AC-shorted, so emitter degeneration is largely removed and the voltage gain magnitude is high. After disconnecting CE, R4 is no longer bypassed and appears in the AC emitter circuit, so the denominator of the gain formula increases. Conclude that the voltage gain decreases.

planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question text to focus on the change caused specifically by disconnecting capacitor CE, not on changing the DC bias network or coupling capacitors.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: For midband AC analysis, a large emitter bypass capacitor shorts the emitter resistor for signal, giving higher gain roughly |Av| ≈ RC/re (or gmRC). If the bypass capacitor is removed, the emitter resistor remains in the AC path, giving |Av| ≈ RC/(re+RE) or gmRC/(1+gmRE), which is smaller.

method.method_draft: First identify CE in the figure as the capacitor shunting the emitter resistor R4. With CE present, AC signal current bypasses R4, so the emitter is nearly at AC ground and local negative feedback is weak. When CE is disconnected, signal current must pass through R4, creating emitter-voltage variations that oppose changes in base-emitter voltage. This stronger emitter degeneration reduces amplification, so the amplifier voltage gain decreases.

planner_metadata.image_role: Read the diagram to see that CE is connected from the transistor emitter node to the bottom reference rail across R4; thus it is an emitter bypass capacitor, not an input/output coupling capacitor. planner_metadata.text_role: Use the wording 'after disconnecting the capacitor CE' as the event to compare the same amplifier before and after the removal of the bypass path.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: An unbypassed emitter resistor introduces local negative current feedback: an increase in emitter/collector current raises emitter voltage, reducing base-emitter voltage variation and suppressing output swing. A bypass capacitor removes this AC feedback by holding the emitter closer to AC ground.
